title: Should bodybuilders do front squats?
summary: NH, who has front squatted weekly for at least two years and calls it his favourite lift, explains why bodybuilders may not want to do it. The front rack is highly technical and regresses quickly, so the lift needs weekly commitment and is a poor occasional variation. Its payoffs are sparing the lower back, building thoracic extension and helping deadlift technique.
claims: The front squat is very technical; its technical rating is about the highest of any knee flexion
In the front rack you grip the bar but the bar rests on the shoulders, held by structure not the hands; it's not an overhead press
Bodybuilders don't need a full grip because they never transition into a jerk; use three fingers (the talon); he has never had the bar roll away
Fewer fingers is easier on elbow and wrist flexibility but less secure; three or four is fine, two is risky
He dislikes the cross-arm front squat: one shoulder sits higher, creating imbalance and shoulder strain, though many bodybuilders use it without injury
The hard part of the front squat is the front rack, not the knee flexion, and it regresses fast if not trained
If you won't front squat at least once a week, don't bother; cycling it every two weeks as a secondary variation wastes time
If you want occasional front squats, do them high volume with a cross-arm grip or on a Smith machine, which removes the stability demand
He learned the front squat from an Olympic weightlifter friend and didn't realise what a time sink it would be
The front squat is punishing: poor form gives wrist tendonitis, which carried over to all his presses
Once he fixed his form the front squat acted as rehab, and his wrist pain on upper body lifts disappeared
Looking back he wouldn't take up the front squat again; he would pick another variation or spend the time elsewhere
Front squats spare the lower back: the load sits in front and the lift forces you to stay vertical, so you can't good-morning it up
The back squat is the lift he has been injured on most; front squats let him keep training legs when his back was hurt and he wasn't weaker on returning
Carryover from front squat to back squat is real but smaller than people think; a pause squat carries over more
Olympic lifters prioritise the front squat because the clean puts them in a front squat position
If you front squat, do it weekly plus one front squat variation (pause, pin, static hold or box) on another day; the variation completes, not replaces
He has two leg days: regular front squats on one, box front squats on the other; they never rotate or he regresses
Front squat progress depends on thoracic extension and the rack, not leg strength; people fail by folding forward
Lumbar rounding is a by-product of thoracic rounding; a strong neutral thoracic spine prevents cat-back deadlifts and lumbar shear
The front squat is the best lift for building thoracic extension
The front squat has almost no strength carryover to the conventional deadlift but helps technique through upper back rigidity
You don't need front squats to grow legs; zercher, reverse SSB squats or unilateral work can replace them
Start front squats light, as a back squat variation, and assess whether the investment is worth it
exercises: bar rests on shoulders; three-finger talon grip; elbows up; stay vertical
spares lower back, builds thoracic extension; high technical demand
uneven shoulders, shoulder strain; fine for occasional high-volume use
front squat variation that completes the main lift
Pause / pin front squat, static hold
more carryover to back squat than front squat
